body.text: It is no secret that China has long sought to replicate the success of Starlink, the satellite internet service, with a domestic solution. As China is closing in on completing its coveted Qianfan Constellation following the launch of 18 satellites into orbit on November 3, this ambition may soon be realized. There are now 274 Qianfan satellites in orbit, still 50 short of the 324 needed for initial service, but the network’s commercialization is nevertheless within reach. Once the constellation is complete, Qianfan is expected to provide high-speed global internet coverage from a low earth orbit (LEO) in direct competition with SpaceX’s Starlink.

Qianfan (千帆, “thousand sails”) is operated by Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology Co., Ltd. (also known as Shanghai Spacecom Satellite Technology, Ltd. or simply Yuanxin Satellite), a nominally private company but with extensive financial backing from several Chinese state entities, including the industrial fund of China Development Bank, the Chinese Finance Ministry, and the Shanghai city government. These links to state capital make Qianfan’s dual-use purpose all but certain.

State involvement is unsurprising given that China’s leadership regards satellite-based systems as a cornerstone of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) continuous transformation into a modern force capable of fighting and winning wars in an “informatized” operational environment. Qianfan could significantly boost China’s space-based military capabilities, particularly those related to tracking, sensing, targeting, and navigation

Beijing’s obsession with an indigenous satellite system stems from its experience during the 1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis. Following Taiwanese president Lee Teng-hui’s visit to the United States in 1995 and ahead of Taiwan’s first direct presidential election, China fired three missiles into the waters off Taiwan to intimidate Taipei. Yet Beijing’s show of force went awry when only one missile hit where intended. The PLA lost track of the other two, reportedly due to the U.S. interrupting GPS services, which forcefully demonstrated Washington’s control over navigation and positioning systems at the time – and Chinese reliance on those same systems. This incident went down as an “unforgettable humiliation” in PLA history, and accelerated the development of BeiDou, along with China’s space industry more generally.

Since then, a growing body of Chinese military and technical scholarship treats satellites as the backbone of modern warfare, a trend that has only intensified in recent years. For example, PLA researchers argued in a 2024 article that “the reliability and availability of positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) information will become the foundational information for missions such as precision strikes, reconnaissance and early warning, as well as command and control.” Building on this, Chinese scholars have identified LEO constellations as a way to strengthen this foundation. Xie Jun, chief designer of the BeiDou satellites, noted that LEO constellations can enhance the accuracy, integrity, and anti-jamming performance of satellite navigation, with military users named among the potential beneficiaries.

In this context, Qianfan deserves special attention. First, according to an August 2026 analysis by the China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI), Qianfan’s satellites have the potential to greatly increase the PLA’s ability to track ships near-continuously using Automatic Identification System (AIS) receivers and relay tracking data to the ground in almost real-time. This would enable the PLA to more quickly identify vessel movement patterns and anomalies, such as positional spoofing, loitering near militarily sensitive sites, or a ship switching off its AIS (“going dark”). Since warships are not required to broadcast their AIS and typically switch it off during operations anyway, this would mainly concern commercial and civilian shipping. Even so, a vessel going dark is itself a signal that can cue radar or optical satellites to take a closer look.

Second, Qianfan can potentially be used in conjunction with other satellite constellations, particularly BeiDou. As Xie Jun’s article suggested, LEO constellations (such as Qianfan) could act as an augmentation layer to make BeiDou positioning more precise and harder to jam. The CASI study also suggested that Qianfan could be layered with the experimental Guanlan Experimental Satellite. It was launched into LEO on November 7 to test “new systems for all-weather, high-precision altimetry readings of global ocean surfaces using a dual-frequency, Ka and Ku bands” and is the precursor to an ocean-observation mission designed to deliver much clearer pictures of the upper ocean’s structure, thus providing a crucial tool in undersea warfare.

Along with other experimental clusters currently underway, whose technology ranges from data routing to imaging, the result would be a vastly more expansive, mutually reinforcing satellite network serving to amplify China’s ability to track a great variety of vessels across the Asia-Pacific, if not the globe.

Finally, Qianfan would be yet another satellite system for the military to draw on during an acute crisis. Beijing’s 14th Five-Year national emergency plan (2021-2025) explicitly calls for unified scheduling of Tiantong, BeiDou, and satellite-internet resources, as well as for an integrated air-space-ground-sea emergency communications network able to function under extreme conditions. In the context of China’s military-civil fusion policy, which seeks greater integration between military and civilian industries, it is conceivable that Qianfan could help amplify China’s existing satellite telecommunication networks should the PLA need to fall back on them in a future crisis.

These developments carry serious security implications for the Pacific region. Most importantly, they threaten to undercut U.S. capabilities at a time when China has become ever more assertive in flexing its military muscle around Taiwan. U.S. naval planning has for decades relied on the ocean’s vastness to keep carrier groups hidden at a distance, and on the ability to deny an adversary the satellite services it depends on. Today, as China is on track to build its own dense web of satellites for tracking, imaging and communications, the United States’ long-standing advantage is dangerously, and quickly, eroding.
